utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. We may now start. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. While we're waiting for the witness, I might alert the Court to our next week's schedule, which has been handed out to Defence lawyers today, and also of a slight change with regard to a witness we had on our schedule for the second week of trial, which we notified Defence counsel about after session yesterday. Witness number 8 on the list of last week we have decided not to call and will not be testifying. That is, I think, consistent with our continuous evaluation of the state of the evidence in an attempt to streamline. Therefore, the witness following witness number 8 on that list, Payam Akhavan, will then be testifying, we hope, by later today. And then we will continue on with the list that we have now provided to the Court and to Defence counsel for next week and later this week as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But the first witness is the one who is now here giving evidence, and we may hope that he will finish today. In this case, we will start tomorrow with number 2 on the new list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Actually, we hope to get to number 2 on the new list today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Today, wonderful. Thank you. We have prepared a list of the dates of hearings, which has been distributed to the parties, and then we will raise a fairly important matter at the end of the cross-examination and re-examination of the present witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Puliselic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that yesterday a minor mistake was made in the transcript on page 130, line 11. It says in the transcript that Dragan Papic said to the witness that it was a Croatian house. That's how it is said in the transcript. But the witness said that Dragan Papic said to the soldiers, who were supposedly there, to not touch that house because that was a Croatian house. So according to the witness, Dragan Papic was addressing the soldiers and not the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you're right, absolutely right. I thank you for your comment, and we will check and make the necessary change in the transcript. Thank you. Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Moskowitz:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, we stopped at about the point that we were going to begin with the events immediately preceding April 16, 1993. Before we get there, I would like to show you a couple of photographs, just so we can better visualise where your house was and some of your neighbours' houses were that you mentioned in your testimony. At this point, I would ask the usher, if he would, to show the witness this exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 76.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, do you see your house in that photograph or what remains of your house, and could you point it out if you do?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see it. It is this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be the house on the left-hand side of that photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the left-hand side. I'm pointing at it with my right hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see another house there that you can identify to the right of your house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is Pero Papic's house here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be to the extreme left on the photograph; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the other side of the photograph, in the distance to the right of your house, is there a house that you can identify?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Sulejman Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that be the house that Abdulah Ahmic lived in?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see Abdulah Ahmic's house in that photograph or is it hidden?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I cannot see it. I cannot see it here. It should be somewhere next to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just so we can correlate the photograph to Exhibit 75, which was the aerial blow-up, perhaps if the usher could show the witness Exhibit 75, the blow-up so he can do that. Your house is house number 37; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The photograph, then, would show your house as house number 37?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I have the usher show the next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number 77.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, do you see the photograph of your house or a picture of your house in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is it. (Indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see two houses directly to the left of your house depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is Pero Papic's house, and I can see Marija's house, Marija Papic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you say Marija Papic's house is directly behind Pero's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could look at the blow-up, Exhibit 75, which the usher will assist you with in a moment, would it be correct to say that "H" and "I" are Pero and Marija's house as depicted in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Marija's house under "I" and Pero's house here, letter "H."

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, once again I don't think that this question has been put correctly. The Prosecutor cannot ask whether it is correct that these houses belong to those specific owners. If the Prosecutor wants to know who these specific houses belong to, then he should ask, "Who do houses under number or letter so and so belong to," otherwise, the Prosecutor is telling the witness both the position and the marks of the houses, as well as the owners' names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moskowitz, I think you should kindly refrain from putting leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: They were leading questions, I certainly admit that, although yesterday we did go through that aerial map, and I believe I asked him whose house was "H" and whose house was "I." He provided that information of his own accord yesterday. This was merely an attempt, I think, to get through this as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps I could raise this with the Defence. As I understood it, there wasn't any dispute about whose house is which. If there is a dispute, then we ought to know. If there's no dispute, then, of course, counsel can lead about it because it's not a matter which is, in any way, contentious. But if it is disputed as to whose house is which, it may be helpful if you would tell the Prosecution so that eventually the Court is going to have an idea of whose house is which and, if necessary, if there's a dispute about it, we would have to decide it, if it's an important matter. Perhaps the Defence might like to put some thought to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ahmic, looking again at Exhibit 75, once again, would you point out the little alleyway or street that you took when you were returning to your home following the October incident and met the Papics, including Dragan Papic, by the machine gun?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I took this direction, this alley. Well, I didn't say that I met Papic with a machine gun. Papic was in the bunker with Simo Vidovic, while Vinko Vidovic and Dragan Papic, they were approaching me from the bunker, and they stopped me somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry for that misstatement. Could you, just for clarity's sake -- I would ask the usher if he would place Exhibit 76, the photograph, on the ELMO so that we can see where that little lane is. This is not a very excellent picture of this, but can you see in that photograph the lane that you were walking down that day, and point it out for us, please?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the lane, towards my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said yesterday that you noticed that there were some blocks that were being used for the bunker that you recognised as belonging to your house. Where did those blocks come from? Were they in front of your house or inside your house or where?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They were brought from in front of my house. The blocks were here in front of my house. They were brought here to Papic's house where they had put up a bunker using the blocks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher. Now, before proceeding on to the next events, I did want to clarify one thing with you that we talked about yesterday, and that has to do with the incident in October '92 and about the barricade. You may have misunderstood my question when I asked you, "What did you know about that barricade situation," and my question specifically to you is, and I want to make it clear, not what did you know personally from what you saw that day, but what you found out about it, either that day or on subsequent days, from talking to people. What do you know about that barricade situation? What had happened on October 20th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I, myself, was not at the barricade; however, I heard from other people talking about it. They said that the barricade was erected by the BiH army close to the cemetery. It was erected by the BiH army, as I heard, because HVO were approaching Novi Travnik from Busovaca or from Kacuni or wherever, but they were told that many HVO troops were approaching because Novi Travnik had been attacked, and that that barricade was put up, yet we were attacked. We were dispersed, and this took only some 60 minutes, 40 minutes. We were dispersed. We were beaten. The HVO took over the whole area. We withdrew and we fled to the upper Ahmici. This is what I heard, but I was not there, and I saw nothing myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether or not, following this incident in which the HVO broke through the barricade and essentially were victorious that day, do you know whether there was any requirement that Muslim citizens of Ahmici turn over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know when they were required to turn over the weapons, but I know that the population of Ahmici were required to turn over the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was requiring them to turn over the weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, their commanders were requiring it. Nenad Santic and -- well, I don't know who else specifically. I just know that the HVO commanders insisted that the weapons be turned over by the BiH army who, anyway, had very few weapons, only the weapons that were brought from Slimeha. When Slimeha was mined at that time, the Territorial Defence went up there to fetch the weapons that were half burnt, destroyed, hardly functional, and they were subsequently repaired. And that's the weapon that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any threats about what would happen if weapons were not turned over that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: There were threats personally. Dragan, on that day, when he was sitting at my table, he said to me, "Unless you turn over the weapons, you'll be shelled. You'll be destroyed," simply, all of us up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This would be Dragan Papic who said this to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Papic told me this in the morning when I came back. We were sitting at the table. He, Vinko Vidovic, my wife, and myself were seated around the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is where Mr. Papic had that bomb fuse and Mr. Vidovic had the card?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was showing me the card indicating that he was a member of the special units of either the Jokers or the police down in the Bungalow. I personally did not touch the card. He would just show it to me, holding it in his hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, following the conflict at the barricade in '92, did you have an opportunity to observe any damage done to the minaret of the mosque located in Ahmici, the lower mosque?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That morning when I took my wife and my children towards Ahmici, I noticed the upper part of the minaret being destroyed. That's the very top of the mosque.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may impose on the usher again, could the witness be shown Exhibits 28 and 29, please? Before you point, just tell us what that is, please. This is Exhibit 28, which has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This was the mosque before. That's the way we built it. When the village was attacked, the upper part, the uppermost part of the mosque was hit, and there were holes caused by the bullets all over the minaret.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next exhibit, please, this would be 29 already admitted into evidence. What does this show, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, these are the holes, and the upper part -- well, probably it's missing because it was destroyed, not the whole minaret, but only the uppermost part that I had shown you on the earlier photograph. This part was not destroyed entirely. It was only the upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this picture accurately show at least part of the damage done to the minaret after the incident?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. This does show some of the damage, but further up, there was a part which was also only slightly damaged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the minaret repaired sometime after the October incident?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It was repaired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to go back to one morning when my wife, when she got up. She noticed through the window my neighbours, the Croats, they were all dressed in camouflage uniforms, and they had weapons with them. At that time, she summoned me to come to the window and have a look. I got up too, and I saw this picture of my neighbours, in weapons, carrying out of Mario Papic's house certain crates, military boxes, crates. What was inside, I do not know, but they were wearing camouflage uniforms, they had weapons. And at that time I told my wife, "Get ready, you and the children, and let's all go to Upper Ahmici. I will, however, stay here to see what was going on." At that time, I knew nothing about what was going to happen, but I noticed, when I went out, there were Ivo Papic, Dragan Papic, Mario Papic, Zoran Papic, all of them were there dressed, with weapons. I went there and I asked the neighbours, "What is going on?" At that time Ivo Papic told me that the Bosnian army had attacked Busovaca, Rovna, Kovacevic, and that a massacre is being committed there. However, I told them that I had no knowledge of that, and I asked them, "What shall I do now?" At that time Ivo Papic said, "There's no life together with you any more. Get lost and beat it to your people up there, and tell Sakib Ahmic," and he was his very good friend, that, "He should never be coming back to me. He shouldn't come here and cry." My wife and my children had left for Upper Ahmici, and after this talk with my neighbours, I decided to go and visit Sakib Ahmic, and I had told him what Ivo had said to me. He simply said, "Well, Fahrudin, I cannot believe this." I turned around and went away, and went up to Urcevihe to stay with my people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an idea of when this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I know they told me when Rovna, Busovaca and Kovacevic was attacked, but I really cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say whether it was before or after the conflict in October?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That was after this first conflict, at the time when we were still living together. At least that's how I can recall it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for clarity too, you mentioned Sakib Ahmic. Which Sakib are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Bajricin's Sakib Ahmic, who was the best friend of Ivo Papic's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is the Sakib who's related to Abdulah Ahmic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was Abdulah's uncle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to focus your attention on the day before April 16, 1993. Do you recall seeing anything unusual that day that raised your suspicions that something might happen the following day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, that day my mother-in-law visited me, with her daughter, and the daughter told me that she had seen two uniformed soldiers on a motorbike. They had camouflage uniforms. One of them had the BiH army flag fixed to the motorbike. They would drive up and down the road. And she also said that they were yelling while driving up and down, and they yelled at her. That day, she went to fetch her other sister, who was married, at the station, in the upper part, and she brought her to my house, together with her child. On the eve, I went out to collect some wood, and my mother-in-law came out too. Marija talked to her. She asked her, "How are you," "What's going on," things like that. After that we went back to the house, and we saw, both my wife, myself and all the others. We saw through the window that Pero's wife had packed her luggage, a car came to fetch her, and she and her child were taking the luggage with them, left for Zenica. However, they couldn't get as far as Zenica because there was a block on the road. Therefore, they had to turn towards Busovaca. My wife, at that time, said, "Something is in the offing, this is no good." However, I told her that I would go up to the upper part of the village, to my commanding officers, and ask them what was the news. And that's what I did. I went up there to the mosque to pray, and on my way to the mosque I met Vinko Vidovic, and I saw him packing up the luggage, the belongings. A car came and his wife and Vinko's children all left. In the mosque, I told my co-believers that the situation was not good. My neighbours were fleeing. They were simply going somewhere. Where, I didn't know. They responded by saying that I was panicking and that I shouldn't cause panic among the people, that I should go home and what did I fear. However, I told them, "I am not afraid, but I have a house full of children and women. I am alone. I'm the only adult male in the house." Their reply was, "If one has to defend one's house, it should be defended at the threshold." When I asked these leaders of mine, they said if I was afraid to sleep down there, that I should go to the upper village. And after prayers, I returned home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to the -- I'm sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I came home, my wife asked me, "What's new?" I didn't say anything. I just said there's nothing. No one knows anything about anything. So we had a talk as to what we should do, because it was difficult for the eight of us to go anyplace. If I didn't have my mother-in-law, and my sister-in-law and the children, I would have gone to the upper village, but as they were staying with us, I stayed at home. We spent the night there, and for my own safety I went outside from 10.00 to 12.00, watching to see whether there were any suspicious movements, any signs that the situation was worsening. I saw nothing. I went back into the house. My wife packed a red bag. I was a bit irritated. I said, "What are you doing? Why are you packing? There's nothing." And she said "Never mind, just in case." And I went to bed. In the morning, I was awakened by the sound of fire. I jumped out of bed, as did my mother-in-law and everyone else in the house. "What is this," she asked. I said, "I don't know what it can be." And she said, "It's a war, children." I ran out to the veranda. I looked around. There was no one. I looked at my neighbours. There was no one. I felt shells falling, all kinds of weapons were being fired, then I went back inside and I said to my wife and children, that they should go into the cellar in case the house were to be shelled, because the upper floor had still not been completed. So to avoid any injury, I told them all to go into the basement where they would be safer. My wife said, "No, we won't go into the cellar, we want to flee into Upper Ahmici." The only thing I said was, "Get out of the house. Don't carry anything, just run towards Upper Ahmici." I stayed behind to lock the house, the cellar, and to look around to see whether there was anyone. While they were fleeing towards the road, I locked the cellar and the house, and I was standing around the corner of my house. I didn't see anyone. And as I was running towards the road, I crossed the road, I turned to the left and to the right, and as I looked to the right, I noticed, next to Ivo's house, two soldiers bending down. I saw the glimmer of fire coming from a firearm from Dragan Papic's window. Then I ran on from there. I caught up with my wife, my mother-in-law, and the children and all the others who were fleeing. When I caught up with my wife, she said, "Take the little girl's back, please." I didn't manage to reach the little girl. I was already hit. When I was hit, I thought -- I said, "Look, I've been wounded. Lie down, everyone." And then I saw, coming from Mehmed Ahmic's and Dragan Papic's house, the shooting was coming from there. From around the corner of Mehmed Ahmic's house I also saw fire coming from a weapon. As I was running with my family, my wife, children, my mother-in-law. We were running towards the upper mosque. And I felt fire coming from up there somewhere, so I knew I couldn't go in that direction. So I ran into Hilmija Ahmic's house, carrying my arm because I thought that it had been broken. When I entered, I saw a house full of women and children. Everybody was asking everybody else what was happening. I laid down on a bench. This was next to the road along which I had come. No one dared help me. I was asking for help, but no one dared to dress my wounds. They were afraid. They just tied up my hand so as to stop the flow of blood. I told them then, "We have no way out, but call UNPROFOR up. They're the only ones that can up to us. We have no other chance." Then Hilmija's daughter-in-law called up Hilmija's daughter, who was a judge in Zenica, telling her to address the UNPROFOR for aid for Ahmici, and that's what indeed happened. She called up. Whether she got her on the phone or not, I can't remember. Later on, my wife asked me whether I needed any assistance. I told her, "Go -- you go and save yourself and the children, and leave me behind." However, she sent her sister to stay with me, and she stayed throughout until the UNPROFOR arrived. When the UNPROFOR arrived, they treated me. They put me on an infusion and they dressed my wounds, intravenous infusion. I asked them to transfer me to the hospital. And there was an interpreter with them. His answer was that they were not allowed to help anyone, because those were the orders they had received from the Croatian army, and they left. I don't know how much time went by. I was lying there. Hilmija's windows had been protected. The windows facing the street were protected with wooden planks five centimetres thick. It was exposed to fire, and they were using incendiary bullets. Regardless of their protection, one of these bullets entered and set fire to a couch, not the one I was lying on, and it started burning. I was alone just then in the room, so I cried out, "The house is on fire." Hilmija and Ismet Pezer entered crawling, crawled in and put out the fire that had started burning. After a little while, the UNPROFOR arrived. This time they took me, and someone else was there, a woman, lying above me. Allegedly it was Nedira Pezer. I didn't say that they took a photograph of me when UNPROFOR was treating me. I forgot to mention that. They took a photograph of me then. And when they transported me to the hospital, they said to me everything would be okay. And on the way there, I think that we were going through the town of Nova Bila, where we were stopped. They wanted to take me to the hospital. There was some kind of misunderstanding. And then they took me to Stari Travnik, to the hospital there, that's where I was treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher to place 75 on the ELMO. Thank you. Just to clarify a few things, Mr. Ahmic, could you, with the pointer, demonstrate the route of travel you and your family took as you fled your house towards Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Along this road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you testified that you got to the road. And did you cross that road, the main road, the Vitez/Bucovaca main road?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I crossed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there an indication on the map, or can you indicate to us about where you think you were when you were hit with the bullet?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Here, between Omer's house and Sakib's stable. Somewhere here between Sakib's stable and Omer's house. That is where it happen. I can't tell you exactly, but there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately where that "X" and arrow is on the exhibit in front of you would be fairly accurate where you were -- accurately show where you were, approximately, where you were struck; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, somewhere just there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What side -- if you can recall, what side of your body was struck with the bullet, your left side or your right side?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: My right arm. This is where the bullet entered, and this is where it came out, and you see what my hand is like now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you still --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is where it entered, and this is where it exited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you struck in any other part of your body with gunfire at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I was struck here in the right hip.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that you went to Hilmija's house. Could you shows us where on this exhibit, after you were injured, where on this exhibit Hilmija's house is?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Here, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that would be house 15 on the blow-up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also said that you saw firing coming from Mehmed's house. Do you see that house on the blow-up in front of you, and if so, could you describe what number it is?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: From here, number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I believe you said you also saw flashes of fire coming from the Papic house. Which Papic house were you referring to, if you could point to it, please?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is Papic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be house marked "A". That would be Ivo Papic's house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, Ivo Papic's. Both Ivo and Dragan live there, Dragan Papic lives there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you armed on that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I never had a firearm. I didn't have a uniform. I felt so sure that I didn't need it, and that this would never happen. At least as far as the Croatian side and the Muslim side were concerned, I could never imagine that this would happen between us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was near you when you were shot in the elbow and in your side? Who were you close to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I remember my wife, that she stopped me, saying, "Please carry this red bag," which the little girl was carrying, and that is when I was hit. And then I said, "Lie down, I have been wounded, they are shooting." And that is when I looked and saw the flash of fire coming from Mehmed's house, and we could hear the shrapnel hitting the iron door of Omer Pezer's house. And they were shooting at me, so I immediately fled from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which house is Omer Pezer's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is here, somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned your wife was near you. Do you recall how she was dressed that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know. I don't know. I know from the photograph I was wearing a sweater, but I do not recall anything about the way people were dressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any children close by you and your wife when you were shot?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember anything, how far from me they were, but they were there, close by. The children, and my wife, and mother-in-law and my sister-in-law, they were all close by. I had reached them. I had caught up with them and when I slowed down, when I reached them, that was when I was hit, when my woman told me to pick up the bag. And before I managed to pick it up, I was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher at this point to show the witness the next photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 78.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I believe this is Exhibit 78, which has been placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, 78.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that picture shows and, if so, please tell us?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I recognise that it was struck with firearms, that it had been burnt. I know that I went inside into this house, and I lay here next to this window against this wall. That is where the couch was, and it went in the shape of a letter "L."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see pockmarks outside that house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I see earmarks left by firearms. Yes, I can see the pockmarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the next series of photographs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I ask you to ask the witness whose house this was?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, whose house is this?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is Hilmija Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have the blow-up right in front of you, Mr. Ahmic, and if you can look at that for a second. Hilmija Ahmic's house, if you could point to it and give us the number on the blow-up?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is number 15. Here it is (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you indicated that some photographs were taken in Hilmija's house. What does this show?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This picture shows me when UNPROFOR came and gave me first aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an idea approximately what time UNPROFOR came?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Approximately at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your family had already fled to upper Ahmici by the time UNPROFOR came; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They had fled to upper Ahmici thanks to UNPROFOR, because they gave them the chance to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could we have the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 80.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, if you could tell us what this picture shows and, perhaps, tell us who these people are in the picture, if you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This was the owner of the house, Hilmija Ahmic. This was his daughter-in-law. This was a neighbour, Pezer, who lived across the road from Hilmija. I don't remember her first name. This is me, and I was being treated. I think that this was the interpreter and, with him, an UNPROFOR officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The interpreter" meaning someone who could speak the Bosnian language with you and you could communicate with to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, who came with the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see that in the photograph the interpreter is dressed like a soldier. Is that how you remember it as well?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could we have the final picture, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 81.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is the same owner, Hilmija Ahmic. He was the owner of the house. And as I just said, this was the, I think, interpreter with UNPROFOR. This is Hilmija's daughter-in-law, and this, I don't know, I can't recognise her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The woman who has her hands on her face, the daughter-in-law, was she the one who called Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, she called Zlatija, Hilmija's daughter, asking her to call up UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a great deal of pain at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Of course I was, because my hand was almost blown off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain conscious that day, all day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I was conscious all the time, even in hospital. I didn't lose consciousness at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of hospital you were taken to in Novi Travnik or in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I was taken to Stari Travnik, the hospital there. The hospital I was accommodated in, there were HVO soldiers, BiH army soldiers. We were all in the same hospital. We were all being treated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you reunited with your family, if you could tell us quickly?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Twenty days later, roughly, I was transferred to Zenica, and when we were being transferred, they used small coaches. I don't remember exactly how many of us there were. The small bus was full. We were stopped at Ovnak. They held us there for an hour. The HVO, their army, they eventually let us go to Zenica, but it was hard. When I was accommodated in the hospital in Zenica, only then did I learn about my wife and children. And then they looked for me in the hospital, and they found me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all right? Did they survive, your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They survived. All of them are okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said that when you were placed in the ambulance, there was a woman in there already. You thought her name was Nedira. Did you have a chance or an ability to observe her injuries at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I couldn't see, but I heard that she had been hit in the head. When I left the hospital, I learned that she had been hit in the head.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to go back for a second to the day before and clarify a couple of things. You talked about a motorcycle going up and down the road the day before. Did you, yourself --

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- see the motorcycle?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it myself. It is my sister-in-law who told me about it when she arrived at my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also talked about meeting Vinko Vidovic on the way to the mosque that evening.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I was heading for the mosque from the road, I saw Vinko Vidovic, his wife, and his children getting ready to leave, and a car was waiting for them to leave. Where they were leaving for, I don't know, but I noticed that they were leaving in the direction of Zenica. And since the road was blocked by stones, they couldn't go to Zenica, so they probably left for Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's what you assume. You don't know that for a fact, is that right, that they were blocked?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say they left for Zenica, in what direction on the valley road would they have to go to go to Zenica, towards the cemetery or towards Vitez?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They started towards the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was the direction that you saw them travel, so you assume they were going to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assumed that they then had to go to Busovaca because they couldn't go to Zenica. You know, a lot of avalanches were there blocking the road, and they couldn't go as far as Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you recall giving a statement to an investigator in 1995 about some of these things?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I recall a statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether you were spoken to for a long time during the time you gave the statement or were you spoken to for a short time or do you recall at all?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can only recall that I was fetched by somebody asking me to make a statement in connection with Ahmici, and I went with them, not knowing what sort of a statement I was supposed to give and why I was supposed to give this statement. However, I went with them. I gave this statement. I cannot recall where I gave it, and I really cannot remember how long I was speaking, because my arm really hurt me. I was in pain. I wasn't focused really. I had lost my house, all of my belongings, and I just couldn't concentrate at that time. I was in pain. As I said before, my arm was really hurting me, and I couldn't focus when I was making this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the investigator speak to you in your language or was he speaking English, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: What language he spoke, I do not know, but there was an interpreter. Whether a man or a woman, I cannot recall either, because I really didn't feel the need. I wasn't focused while giving the statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall, one way or the other, whether the statement was read over to you after you gave your statement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall that. It may have been read to me, but I really cannot remember that. I cannot remember anything about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you now had a chance, in the last several days, to review and look at that statement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have had an opportunity to do it. I saw it. I reviewed it, and I was shocked by the statement, because what is said in the statement, it really causes pain in me, because I have really had very many unpleasant experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you think that there were some mistakes in the statement, as you read it over recently?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When the attorney was reading this statement to me, I noticed mistakes, and there are things in the statement that I had never said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are there some things you specifically recall now that you think were mistakes in the statement that you would like to clarify at this point?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the situation when I was wounded is concerned, that's where I was really confused. I could never get to Hilmija's house with my family. I couldn't get into the house. I supposedly asked the commanding officer to give me a weapon or something. I really cannot understand why this is in the statement, because I could never say this. I was not wounded there. I was not there with the family. I ran into this house on my own.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you're referring to a sentence in the statement that indicates that you had gone to Hilmija's house before you were wounded, left Hilmija's house and then were wounded after leaving Hilmija's house, and then returned again. You're saying that that is just not accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May I have just one second, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Those are all the questions I have. At this point, we would offer into evidence Exhibits 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, and 81, I believe, are all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, I would like to put a few questions to this witness myself, and then Petar Puliselic will be cross-examining this witness. However, it is about ten minutes until the break, and the ten minutes will not be enough for my questions. Therefore, I would ask you to advise me on further deliberations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. We will rise now so that we will resume at twenty past eleven, and you will start with the cross-examination. It's better for you and, of course, for the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic. Cross-examined by Mr. Pavkovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Petar Pavkovic. I'm an attorney.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to put a few questions to you. Yesterday in your testimony you said that you were born in 1953 in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you spent all your life there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, except when I was working for three years and a half in Rijeka on a construction job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the relations among the different ethnicities and neighbours, or rather, more specifically, the first question, what ethnicities were living in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as ethnicity is concerned, I was really not thinking a lot about it. I was not paying a great deal of attention to that fact. There was no need for me to do that. We lived together very well. I was not interested in the ethnicity, I just took a person at face value. We lived together -- I mean, I can't imagine any community to living a better life. I know that we would marry with people from other ethnicities, and I never really noticed who is who and who was who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you and the other citizens were in good relations?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. With all of them. With Croats, with all the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you said it yesterday, this went on until 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was actually going on at that time? What did you notice?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I noticed something I never saw before. I saw for the first time these camouflage uniforms with my neighbours, and I noticed that they were procuring weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time you were at war with the Serbs. What was unusual about it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that there was a war going on at that time, but -- how to put it. I didn't understand it as a war. I was simply not interested, because I was against any war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time had you recognised that there had been a war in the former Yugoslavia, in Slovenia and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that. I knew a war was waged. How and why, however, I didn't know why. I was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask anyone living together in a good life what was going on?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Of course, I was asking them. I would ask my neighbours, "What is going on. Why is there a war?" And they would simply say, "The Serbs had attacked."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And on one day you were told to join your people, to beat it, as you said yesterday. How did you understand that? Before that you had joint duty guards and everything, and then all of a sudden you were told to go and join your people.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they told me, but I didn't understand it. I just went up to join my people. I would join them, and we would then organise duty guards which were not really very specific. It was not really duty guard. We would sit down, we would play cards, we would play chess. We actually were just together to prevent a possible incident, an unusual situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, since when had you been a member of the BiH army in relation to the events in 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: In April, 1992, I would join the defence, the Territorial Defence, because I was put on a waiting list by my employer, and I had to bring to my company certain certificates to show them that I was incorporated into an organised unit and that I would get salary from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand you. You said you went up there with your people. Where was that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That was up there in Krcevine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you report at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Bilic Hidzo was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, he was sort of a commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort after commander?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't interested in that. There was some sort of commanders in charge of guards and I was a member of that guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many commanders of this sort were there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, I know there was Pjanic, then there was Hidzo Bilic and Ahmic Muris. I can recall these commanders. When they were there and how long, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were the commanders. Whose commanders? Who did they command to?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know they were in contact with Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in Krcevine how many other people were there that they were in contact with?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand me? You are talking about a commander. Well, if you are a commander, then you have certain people to command to. Who were they commanding?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, these were actually not commanders. These people were in charge of deploying the guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice them having any weapon when you came there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, they had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No weapons whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the weapons that were collected at Slimena and were brought in?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This were burnt up weapons that were sent to Grabovi and Upper Ahmici. The people who went up to Slimena, they brought the weapons back. They would repair the weapons so that they can be functional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me a name of these people who went and fetched the weapons, repaired them?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Suad Ahmic was one of them that I know. I know he went up there and brought the weapons back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see the weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never saw a single piece of the weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now go back to the situation prior to the first conflict. You told us how this first conflict took place. I'm referring to the October, 1992 conflict.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were given orders by the BiH army to put up a barricade. Well, not you personally, but that the order was issued by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as this barricade is concerned, I told you before that I received no orders. I knew nothing about a barricade being erected. I was not on the barricade. I heard from other people talking about the barricade, when it had already been put up, when this was all over, and they told me that Novi Tavnik was attacked, that many troops would have to go there to attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who then received this order?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that it was issued -- sorry, that the barricade was erected by the BiH army, that's what I heard, but I specifically know nothing about this barricade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who you heard this from?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall this. This was a story that went on. I heard it. By whom and when, I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who exactly, according to your knowledge, put up this barricade?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was the BiH army that put it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were these people from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I heard that two of them were from Ahmici, Zado Ahmic (phoen) and another Ahmic. Well, these two, but nobody else, I heard, was participating in the erection of the barricade. And I heard that they took weapons from somebody at the barricade, but what specifically happened I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that later this barricade was removed in about an hour's time.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I heard, the barricade was removed rather quickly, in an hour or an hour and a half, as I heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the removal of the barricade, did you go there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I never went to that site ever. I don't know where the barricade was put up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know how it looked like?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know how it looked like. I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that on the 20th of October, 1992, Halid Pezer was killed and that you transferred his body to his mother.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly the date when it was, but I can recall coming down there. Whether it was a day or two after the attack, I don't know, but I know that I went down there with Mirsad Ahmic, who was my uncle, a relative. I heard there that this man was killed, and that his mother was asking for the body to be discovered. I don't know where the body was. Mirsad told me where it was, and we went there together. We took the body out and transported him to the mosque. We left it there and this is where the mother collected him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned a name Ahmic. Are you referring to the same person? Now, earlier ago you talked about Halid Pezer?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Halid Pezer was killed, but Mirsad Ahmic was with me. He was with me transporting the body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was the body of Halid Pezer at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It was behind Pjanic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is where he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that this is where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure but this is where we found him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen him being killed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the first conflict -- I think it is better for me to use that term than to mention dates.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this first conflict, you said that the Bosniaks were requested to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who made this demand? Did anybody ask you to surrender your weapons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It was the HVO that demanded it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HVO, yes, but a person, a person you know?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I heard this from our leader Muris Ahmic, who was there where we kept watch duty. And when we were attacked, I think this was on the next day, he asked that our weapons be surrendered to the Croats because they had threatened to destroy us all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you then keeping watch duty?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: At that time I was in Gornji Ahmici, Upper Ahmici. I don't remember for how long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of you were there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Not many. We were just local, 10 or 15 local inhabitants, because some people were fighting the Serbs on the front, some were working. There weren't many of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that some sort of a front-line, a combat line?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't have any combat lines anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please refer back to the events on the eve of the second conflict, when you were wounded, as you just explained. You said you were woken up in the morning by the sound of gunfire, and that then you were getting ready with your family. I'm summarising what you said, of course.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That with your family you headed towards the house of Hilmija Ahmic. Tell me, you explained to us today that while you were going towards Hilmija Ahmic's house and when you caught up with your family, which went ahead of you, and when your wife told you to pick up a red bag from the little girl, as you've said, that you were hit then and wounded. Did I understand you well that your wife was there as well?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They were all nearby, my wife, my family, my mother-in-law, my sister-in-law. They were all going in front ahead of me, and I caught up with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time could this have been?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: About 5.20, 5.30. This was at the time of the morning prayers, when we go to prayer, when we do our religious rights.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You showed Their Honours the injury you sustained on that occasion. After being taken by UNPROFOR on that same day for treatment, where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I was in a personnel carrier. I didn't know where they were taking me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in the end where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I assumed it was Nova Bila, where they took me inside -- or rather, they opened the personnel carrier. There was a misunderstanding. I don't know what happened. Then they shut the door again and then continued on. However, when we reached this spot where they opened the carrier again, realised that I had got -- I had reached Stari Travnik, in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Roughly 20 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: After that they didn't do anything to me. They didn't treat my arm. They just put a splint on it, because the hospital had been looted, there were no plates, no spoons. I ate from cardboard containers with my hands. There were no spoons, no plates, no pyjamas. For six days I laid there with nothing on me. I had nothing on me. And I spent about 20 days there. They couldn't do anything for me. And then they said they would transfer me to Zenica, and that's what they did. A small bus collected us and took us, via Han Bila, to Obloke, where again we were stopped by Croatian HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us when you reach the Zenica hospital.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they admit you immediately into hospital?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did, immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind, just roughly?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Approximately a month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they do surgery?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. My arm was infected, because in Travnik they didn't have the necessary bandages. They didn't have the medicines. And when I got to Zenica, Mr. Sabic, the doctor, told me that my arm was infected and that they couldn't help me either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, my hand remained stiff. I had terrible pains for two or three months after that. I had constant pain because everything was broken there in my elbow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when were you discharged from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I left the hospital. I went to the infirmary, outpatient's department. I did exercises and thermal treatment. Then I went to the medical school. I don't remember how long I stayed there. After that, I asked them to give me an apartment where I could stay with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question only has to do with the time you spent in various medical institutions.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember, but there is the evidence. There is my file, my documents, showing how much time I spent in hospitals. All that is in the documents. I can't remember the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. We were talking in general terms. I'm asking you about the approximate period. Did you say that you had very severe pains for another two or three months?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I had severe pains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when was your treatment completed? When did you go home?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was all over. I can't remember all that, but there are the documents. There are the medical records to show that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you if you remember without the documents. Tell me, after those three months, shall we say, that you had severe pains, did you continue to have pain?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. My arm hurt for three years until it all healed, because nothing was really undertaken, and I still have problems with that arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you please now answer this question, and, Mr. President, this will be my last question. Today you have already partly answered this question, but tell me, apart from your testimony yesterday and today in this honourable Trial Chamber, how many times and with whom did you discuss these events in Ahmici of the 16th of April, 1993, the second conflict?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. Of course we talked about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is how many times and with whom? I do not mean with your neighbours, but with persons who introduced themselves as representing a certain institution or a body, with official persons?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I remember talking twice to representatives of our own authorities who asked me to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you spoke to people who told you that they had come on behalf of the International Tribunal, the Prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do remember that they came, but I don't remember when, because I was traumatised. I was wounded. Everything I owned had been destroyed. My arm was bothering me, so I really can't remember. I wasn't always very willing to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume, Mr. Ahmic, that you still feel traumatised to this day, even today?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Of course. I don't like talking about it, because it upsets me every time I talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, Mr. Ahmic, but as you said at the beginning of your testimony, we need to learn what you saw, what you experienced, what you heard. So I hope you will understand us and me personally when I'm questioning you about these details which are still upsetting you. Will you tell me, please, do you remember -- maybe I could refresh your memory. Did you, two years after the event, that is, in 1995, did you make a statement to a person who said that he was an investigator of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Sir, I really do not remember. I know I made statements, but I cannot fix it in time. I didn't consider this. I did make statements, but I didn't think that it would come to this in concrete terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when you learned that all of this would take place, did you then talk to anyone?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I never talked, nor did I write anything. I'm saying what I experienced, what I remember, and this is the truth. What I know and what is in my head, that is what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to remind you of some statements that you made earlier on, and we have those statements in writing, signed by you, to remind you of some of the things you said, would that refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if necessary, I should like to tell you where I'm quoting from, even though I have the Croatian version here, but I can refer you to the English text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the part where you mention Halid Pezer, that you wanted to carry his body to his mother, that you were picking him up from a trench?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't see a trench, nor was there a trench. Halid was lying on the ground. Two soldiers were present there. I don't know them. I don't know who they were. We were in fear. We feared they would do something to us. I simply said that we picked him up. And there was no trench, nor did I see any trench.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just remind you that in this statement, maybe I should have done that at the beginning, this statement from the 7th of February, 1995, you say that this is your only statement. Now you've told me that you made several statements.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't understand you. You used the Croatian word "vejlaca" for February.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's the second month, February.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat: On the 7th of February, 1995, you told the investigator of the Office of the Prosecution that this was the only statement that you had provided up to then, but you have just told me that you made several statements. What is correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I remember very well that I came once or twice to the security office or to Metalurg Company and that I was questioned, and that is the truth, but I don't know when that was. But I was interviewed. Why I was interviewed, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I beg the Court for indulgence. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain, I didn't quite understand what you meant when you said "CSB"?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is our police down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They took me there. Where they came from, I don't know who it was, and they took me there to make a statement to those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After making that statement, you read it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I didn't read it. I don't remember them reading it to me either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I signed it. I saw that I had signed it, but I really do not remember anything. I was depressed. My arm was hurting, and when I talked about it, it upset me, and I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this was two years after the event when you were wounded. You said that your pain lasted for three months, but this was two years later when you made this statement?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I had constant pain for three months, day and night. I couldn't sleep during the day or the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, sir, you made the statement two years after you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember them reading the statement to me. I don't remember them translating it into Bosnian for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me remind you. If I remind you, perhaps you will remember. You said today and yesterday that you were wounded going to Halid's house. When you and your wife, after the second conflict, went towards Halid's house to accommodate your family there, that you were wounded then. That is what you said today.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we are not understanding one another. I'm talking about the second conflict. Early in the morning of the 16th, you were taking your family, your mother-in-law and the children, to Halid's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, not to Halid's house, Hilmija's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that is when you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, when we were trying to escape from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what you said in 1995? May I read it out to you? You said, and I quote: "When my family was put up in this house, I decided to look for my leader, my commander. I did not have a weapon with me, so I thought maybe he could give me a weapon. I was wounded as I was leaving Hilmija Ahmic's house, and I was hit in the right elbow." Today you explained that you were also hit in another part of your body?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the difference between what you said here in court and what is written down here?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do see the difference, and this has upset me a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has upset you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This has upset me because that is not what I said under any circumstances, and I do not remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Only when I came here and when my attorney showed me this statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said you came here, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I came here to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what attorney?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: My Alberto. He showed me that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This statement from 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The statement that you are quoting from, he showed me that statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did he show it to you? Did he read it out to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I asked him to read it out to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did an interpreter read it for you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: He read it and the interpreter translated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: What happened was that I said, and that is true, that I do not remember any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't understand that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I said that I do not remember anything from that statement. I do not remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what you have told us here in court, how come you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I remember that because that is the truth. I told you the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Tribunal things that mostly figure also in this statement. I have just drawn attention to certain differences. So my question is how come there is this difference and why is this not correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know how this happened. I don't remember how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else did the person whom you call your attorney tell you? What else did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: He told me just to tell the truth and the things I saw. "Don't say anything else."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he show you any photographs?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. He showed me the photographs on which I was wounded and the maps and things. He did show me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavkovic. Mr. Puliselic? Cross-examined by Mr. Puliselic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good day, sir. I'm attorney Petar Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that the Bosniaks and the Croats, at first, held joint guard duty?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
