utterances.text: Do you remember, approximately, when the Bosniaks and Croats started holding separate guard duty, roughly?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Roughly, I really don't know. I know that, with my neighbours, I held guard duty below the road. We never crossed the road. And I know that on one occasion, Rafael Skoro told me, "I'm really sorry, but we can't keep watch duty together anymore. Go and join your people."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the event when a barricade was put up in Ahmici in 1992. You said that you were not present there.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, know that in the area of Jajce, there was a battle between the Serbian forces and the HVO, that is, between the Serb army and the HVO? Do you also know that the HVO needed assistance in men because Jajce was about to fall?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of that because the war simply -- I didn't realise that the war was coming, that there would be a war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the road that leads to Jajce, because apparently HVO units were moving in the direction of Novi Travnik. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any prior knowledge to the effect that the Bosniaks or the Muslims would be putting up that barricade in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You're speaking in Croatian. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone inform you? Did you hear anything about it, that this barricade would be put up?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I said that after all this, after this barricade, I was not informed. I didn't know there was a barricade, because later when I went to the village, I heard that there was a barricade and that it had been put up by the BiH army. Because they apparently had heard that Novi Travnik had been attacked, and that large numbers of HVO troops were coming from Busovaca, Kacuni, and I don't know from where else, but that a very strong army was heading for Novi Travnik. And that the barricade had been put up by the BiH army to stop those soldiers. That is what I heard. So that within one hour or an hour and a half, they had captured this village afterwards and passed through unimpeded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember exactly when it was you took your family to upper Ahmici? You said that this was in the morning when the shooting started. Could it have been the evening before?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I remember both conflicts occurred just when we were praying. Both conflicts started at the time of the morning prayer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, but I'm asking you whether, perhaps, your family had been taken away the evening before, before the shooting started early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I was with my family at home when both conflicts broke out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that your closest neighbour was Alija Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Among the Muslims, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he the closest among the Muslims or is he the closest generally?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Among the Muslims, he's the closest, and Marija is the closest among the Croats, and Pero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that his son was Abdulah?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, the son of Alija Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does he have any other son?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: He had Muris and Munir, both of whom were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Muris?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Muris, at the time of the first attack, was the leader, the leader of our guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember exactly, was it Muris who actually informed you that the barricade would be put up?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, nobody informed me. I didn't even know anything about it. I just told you. I don't know anything about the barricade. I only could have heard about it from others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that at the time of the first conflict, Halid Pezer had been killed. And you said in the statement you gave to the investigator that he was hit by a sniper. My question is: How do you know that it was a sniper that had killed him?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I assume, because he was hit by a single bullet, single shot, but I don't know what weapon was used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're only assuming that it was a sniper?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that any Croat was killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember any Croat having been killed. I don't know. I never heard that any Croatian soldier had been killed on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement you made to the investigator, you spoke about burnt houses, and, among other things, you said that Mehmed Ahmic's house, Hajrudin Pjanic's, Sakir Pezer's and Mehmed Ahmic's house had been burnt. You also mentioned four stables, and you listed the owners of those stables that had burnt during the first conflict. Was that just so?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is true that I said that Alija's stable, Mehmed's house, Bilic's stable, and I don't remember those others that I listed. I know that Alija Ahmic's, Mehmed Ahmic's, Hidzro Bilic's house, I certainly listed them, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the information available to the Defence, it was only one house that burnt, the house of Mehmed Ahmic, known as Sudzuka, and partly Hajrudin Pjanic's and Sakir Pezer's stable. A witness has also testified to that here in the courtroom during the hearings. What do you think is correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: What I just said is correct. I listed the houses that were burnt, but I don't remember exactly all the houses that I listed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you remember fully your statement regarding the number of houses and stables that were burnt?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember the number of houses and stables.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Can you, perhaps, answer the following question: How many members of the BiH army were there in Ahmici, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Approximately, I don't know. There weren't any members of the army. This was no army. There was no command. According to my understanding, people just acted as they wanted on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the situation similar with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was not. They had a command, and they acted strictly in accordance with their orders, as far as I could notice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also followed certain orders as to who should go where for which duty?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. The leader of the guard duty did make a timetable as to when we should keep watch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a statement to the investigator, you said that Dragan Papic came to see you one day in order to inform you that you should contact Slavko Skoro. Yesterday during the hearing, you said something else. You said that Vinko Vidovic and Dragan Papic stopped you when you were returning home, and that they told you on that occasion that you should contact Slavko Skoro. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It is true that they stopped me right next to the bunker built with my building blocks, and there was a light machine gun there, which could be put on a support and which could also be used without this support. I also saw Simo Vidovic there, Dragan Papic. And Vinko Vidovic came up to me when I was passing with my family and told me that I had to ask permission from Slavko Skoro to return to my home for reasons of security.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that that is different from what you told the investigators?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is what I said, and this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, who is Vinko Skoro?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Vinko Skoro, it's not Vinko Skoro. It's Vinko Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Dragan Papic said that you should contact Vinko Skoro?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, Slavko Skoro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. Who is Slavko Skoro?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Slavko Skoro was one of their leaders, a commander. I don't know who was under his command or leadership, but I know that he was there in that capacity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that Mehmed Ahmic's house was shot at from Dragan Papic's house, but then you said you didn't see it. You heard about it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was behind Sakib Bajric's stable on the road. The two of them, I don't know who exactly was with me, but they told me that Mehmed Ahmic is in his house with a family, that shots are being fired from both the forest and Dragan's house at his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I remind you that this is also something that you did not make in your statement you gave to the investigator in 1995, these details.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have also mentioned yesterday in this court an M-53 machine gun, and you also mentioned a bunker that was put up from concrete blocks that had belonged to you and that had been around your house.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me emphasise on this occasion again that this was not mentioned by you in your statement to the investigator in 1995.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I guess not. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you perhaps tell us what did this machine gun look like, what is the size of the bullets, the calibre?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: This is the machine gun I was given in the army. It is a machine gun you could use with a support and without it. When you use the support, you need three gunners. I was one of the three while I was at the army. And when you use it with a support, it can be an anti-aircraft gun. It is also possible to be -- well, it has to be operated by one person. It has to be carried out by another person. Well, anyway, that's how I -- what I thought was the type of the weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of metres, how far was the machine gun away from you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I saw it from the road, about 30 metres away. Well, roughly, of course. I don't know exactly how far away it was from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this machine gun surrounded by the concrete blocks, by the bunker? Was it put up outside the bunker?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, the bunker was in a semicircle. The machine gun was located down here. So I could see it in front of the bunker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of the day was it approximately, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. It may have been around noon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you answer the following question: At that time, and I'm referring to 1992, did the Muslims in Ahmici set up a combat line? To be more specific, you used this very term, the "combat line", in the statement you gave to the investigator of the International Tribunal, so tell me, what is a combat line? What was this combat line?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I just know that there were no combat lines in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigator, you said that Muris Ahmic, the commander, came to the combat line and asked from those who were located at the combat line something. Can you recall this? Can you recall Muris Ahmic coming there?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember the watch guard. We were just watching there. It was not a combat line. And he came there when he insisted that we surrender the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of weapons did you have at that time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I had no weapons whatsoever. I never had a weapon. I never had a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking you about the weapon. Did you have the weapon then?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the point in you being watch guard without a weapon?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: With Hajrudin Pjanic, I told him that I will have no weapon. And actually, I didn't want to join the watch guard because I had no weapons. Usually the people would not use the weapon on watch guard, they would just keep them in their houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said you were somewhere around Sakib Ahmic's stable, and that two neighbours told you that shots being fired from the forest and from Papic's house. You didn't mention this to the investigator either. How can you explain that.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It turns out that your recollection now is much better than it was in 1995. Yesterday you also said that on one morning Dragan Papic and Vinko Vidovic came to your house, and that Dragan Papic was holding in his hand some sort of bomb fuse?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This, again, is a new detail that you mentioned -- did not mention in your statement to the investigator. How come?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that. I felt the need now to tell to this Tribunal everything that I can remember, all the details I can recall in order to be able to tell the truth and the whole truth here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to another distinction. Earlier ago, you did not, in a single word, say that Dragan Papic threatened saying that the Croats would destroy the other part of Ahmici, while you said this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I say yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your statement to the investigator, you said that when you left Hilmija Ahmic's house you were wounded?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you said that when you were hit, you saw a flash of a rifle shot from a window of Ivo Papic's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that. Well, you can't see a flash from there really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that is what you said in your statement.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't recall this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is the distance between Hilmija Ahmic's house and Ivo Papic's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, try to give me an approximate figure.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, about 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I think you are right. However, in your statement to the investigator, you mentioned 100 metres. What is the distance between Ivo Papic's house and the site where you were wounded, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately I can perhaps say that it is some 40, 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that upon being wounded you were resting in Hilmija Ahmic's house, and you said that the windows of the house were protected?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other hand, however, in your statement to the investigator, you said that from Hilmija Ahmic's house you could see soldiers running around Ivo Papic's house, and you described them, the soldiers. You said that they had camouflage uniforms, you said that they had some socks on their head, with openings for eyes and mouths.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I do not remember that. I was wounded. I was lying down. I couldn't see that in any way. I was lying down. I was wounded in my arm and my thigh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'm just drawing your attention to the differences between the statements you made here in the Court and the statement you gave to the investigator. After Hilmija Ahmic's house, what were the other houses close to your house, and I'm referring to the Muslim houses only.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Only Alija Ahmic's and Sulejman Ahmic's. And further up towards the road there was Salih Ahmic's brother's house, and Salih Ahmic's house and Mirnes Ahmic's, who were the brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a number of Muslim houses together. I will go back with one question to 1992. Can you answer the following question: On October 20, 1992, near your house were there any soldiers that were shooting at Pero Papic's house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That's true. In the morning when the attack was launched, when I went out with my wife and my children, when we were heading towards Upper Ahmici, Pero and Vinko told me that their windows had been shot at. And it's true that one could see traces of shots on Pero Papic's windows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you could see the damage?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. Who was shooting, where from and how, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today, in your testimony, you said that when you had given the statement to the investigator of the International Tribunal, you felt some pain in your arm and that you were not focused?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, these details that I reminded you of that were mentioned in your statement were now denied by you. You said that what is in this statement and these differences that I've been pointed at, you said that you did not make this -- these statements to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember it. Maybe I gave the statement, but I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were not concentrated. Why didn't you tell the investigator about it, this fact, if that was true?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I would just answer the questions that were put to me specifically. Whatever was asked of me, I answered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read to you a text at the end of the statement you gave to the investigator. It reads as follows: "This statement has been read over to me in the Bosnian language and is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." This is a statement you signed?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw that I had signed it, but I really do not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness, and I would like to submit this statement as evidence, the statement made by the witness to the investigator of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 2/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I assume the Defence are through with their cross-examination, and I wonder whether the Prosecutor -- yes, Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I shall be very brief, as my learned colleagues have covered almost all the questions I had. May I mention the name now? Is it an open or a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It's an open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, in that case I will not mention the name. Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, what your signature on this statement you gave to the investigator meant to you? The fact that you signed this piece of paper, what did it mean to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I made that statement. I don't remember, because I was upset by that war. I was hurt. I made a statement, but I simply don't remember anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is: Could you explain to the Court what the fact of signing that paper meant to you. What went through your mind when you signed that paper?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Nothing. I simply don't know. I simply signed it, because they brought me there to make the statement. I made the statement and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it means. I signed it. It means that I made a statement, that I signed it, but why, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The interpreter explained to you that what you signed meant that what is in that statement was yours?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the translator explaining that to me, nor do I remember him translating that into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any medical documentation about your treatment?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I think I do. I think that the attorney has all the medical reports. He showed me them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because these documents were not disclosed to us?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't give them anything. They themselves got it. How they got it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they showed you that it was in their possession?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that they have something that they haven't disclosed to us. You're quite sure that they showed it to you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. They do have it and they showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The doctors who were treating you, when did they tell you that they had done everything that they could, and that they could not achieve any further improvement with your arm? When did they tell you that? Yes, that they wouldn't treat you any further.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I reached the hospital in Zenica. Then Dr. Sabic told me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but you were still treated for a time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was, for a long time. I don't remember exactly. I know that I was in the hospital in Zenica, then in the outpatients department, then also in the medical school, but for how long I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But when did you leave the last medical institution in which you were treated?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I don't remember when I left the medical school, because I stayed there too. I don't remember when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the therapy they gave you?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I went for heat treatment, exercises, electricity, ice and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever treated for depression?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you just told the Court that you were depressed, but you were never treated for depression?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. I was deeply affected by the war, by having lost everything, and for a long time I was fearful as a result of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You never went for psychiatric treatment?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't need that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't understand in your statement that you gave to the investigator, the Prosecution, you said that, "During the attack I was a member of the BiH army," without saying whether you were referring to the first attack on the 20th of October, '92, or the second on the 16th of April, '93. As of when did you consider yourself to be a member of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I considered myself to be a member from April 1992. That is when I joined, because of the certificates I carried to my company to be able to certificate the fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we've heard all that. You need not repeat that. We know that and it is already in the transcript. So if I understood you well, you considered yourself to be a member of the army from April '92?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: A member of what we had, this defence. That is what it was. This watch duty that we kept, that is what it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but from when did you consider yourself to be a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: That is when I joined.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you put an equation sign between membership in the Territorial Defence and membership in the army, as far as I understand.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Well, that was something like that. It was called the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we've cleared that up now. When you use the pronoun "we," you said, "We put up the barricade on the main road in Ahmici," and it follows from this statement that you participated in putting up the barricade.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I did not. I did not participate, I only heard about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why then did you use the pronoun "we"? Were you thinking of the Bosniak side without your participation, or were you implying that you too participated?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that the BiH army had put it there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you considered this having been done by the party -- by the side you belonged to, but you were not present. I apologise, Your Honours, but I feel that it is necessary to clear these points up. Then you said, "We were supposed to prevent the passage of Croatian soldiers through Ahmici." Again you use the word "we." I assume you mean your Bosniak side was to prevent the passage of Croatian soldiers through Ahmici, but you personally did not participate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further on, you said that you were told to report to Slavko Skoro, and you didn't report to Slavko Skoro?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer any consequences for not reporting to Slavko Skoro?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went on to say that you saw Hakija Trako?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, I didn't mention him. Not Hakija, Jahija. Jahija Trako. Jahija Trako.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, witness, you said Hajika. I apologise. Jahija Trako said that they were collecting rifles and handing them over to the Croatian side. Then you went on to say, "I know the main people who surrendered their weapons were killed in the second conflict." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The people that you were down there next to the road, below the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Jahija Trako? Was he below the road?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, he was not. He was in Upper Ahmici and he's alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that on the eve of the conflict, we're talking about the 15th of April now, that you first went to see your commander, Hajrudin Bilic, nicknamed Hadzija and you told him and warned him of the danger that was coming that you yourself had seen?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take your warning seriously?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No. No one knew anything about anything. No one knew anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that you went to the mosque and you told everyone what you had seen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went to two places and you made these warnings in two places?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reaction of the people in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No one knew anything. In fact, they attacked me and said I shouldn't cause panic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the people in the mosque?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: There was the Hadzija who was killed. I know the person who built the mosque. Then there was Ahmic who was killed, Abdulah Ahmic who was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't mind about the names, I just want to know whether there were any people who had come from Krajina?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any outsiders there, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Roughly how many people were there around the mosque at the time?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: At the time mostly elderly people, five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Altogether?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Altogether.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were speaking about the camouflage uniforms that individual Croats were wearing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the uniform worn by the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The BiH army, as far as I recollect, did not have uniforms, but what they would bring from Slimena, canvas from the Yugoslav army, the JNA, and then they made uniforms from that material, but they didn't have any uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But what they made from that material, what colour was it?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It was camouflage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was no distinction between them in terms of the colours?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, this material was different. It was different in colour from the camouflage uniform. There was a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I won't ask you anything about the machine gun, because you explained it very well. You're the only one among all those who spoke about a machine gun so far. Now, let me go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but we feel that you are counsel for Zoran Kupreskic, and we don't see the relevance of all the questions you are putting to the witness. If you go on putting a lot of detailed questions concerning matters which are of relevance to those accused who have been mentioned by the witness, then, as I say, it is a Pandora's box. We will never come to an end of this trial. I wonder whether you could exercise some restraint and refrain from putting questions -- we have already allowed Mr. Pavkovic to ask questions, although his client, Vladimir Santic, to the best of my understanding, has not been mentioned by the witness. But as I say, we can't allow all counsel to put a lot of questions. The more so, because some counsel have already questioned or put in doubt the credibility of the witness, and have put a lot of questions about the written statement. I wonder whether it is of some utility. I mean, whether it is useful for this trial to keep insisting on some points. Although you don't repeat the same points made by your colleagues, you go on insisting on the same matters. May I suggest that we break now for lunch and we resume in two hours, and then I hope that you will -- if you wish to go on you will go on, but we will now, over the weekend, think of some sort of regulation to be looked at. Something to be issued so that we -- without restricting in any way the right of the Defence to cross-examine the witnesses, whether we can come to some sort of balanced and sensible solution so as to avoid protracted proceedings, which in the event may not prove useful. I wonder whether after that the Prosecutor wishes also to re-examine the witness, so we can make some plans for the afternoon. Mr. Moskowitz, do you intend to re-examine at the end of -- well, of course you can't say now, you are not sure, a hundred per cent sure, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I had two short clarifications I want to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: So you also intend to re-examine. So that's why it's better to rise now, and we will reconvene at what, quarter to three, I think, so we have two full hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I have come to the end of my cross-examination, but before the Prosecutor starts with the re-examination, I should like to explain why all Defence counsel are cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. All right. So you'll do so this afternoon. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m. . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Before I call upon Mr. Radovic, let me tell him that I owe him an apology for speaking in a slightly impatient tone before lunch when commenting on his cross-examination. I, however, stick to the substance of what I said, and we may probably have an exchange of views or a discussion on this point. I wonder whether Mr. Radovic would now like to address this particular point, as he announced before lunch.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm referring to two matters. As far as the Defence counsel's questions are concerned, we decided that Mr. Petar Pavkovic, who is our coordinator, will raise this issue. However, there is another problem. The problem that as far as the last witness is concerned, the Prosecution's office never submitted to us their medical records. We would ask the Court to request the Prosecutor to submit these medical records to us for the following reason: The witness said that, given the pain suffered two years after the wounding, due to the wounds that were inflicted on him, he was not in a position to make a correct statement, if you will, to the investigators of the OTP. Given the fact that two years is a very long period of time, we would like to submit these medical records to a forensic medical expert so as to establish the authenticity of the records concerned. This is why we would need the medical records concerned. The other issue will be taken up by attorney Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: On this particular point, the Court considers that this is a small, unimportant issue, not relevant to the question of credibility of the witness. So we don't even need to ask the Prosecutor to comment, and we will move on to other matters. I would turn to Mr. Pavkovic to raise the issue of cross-examination, the general issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for allowing us to raise these issues too. The question you raised today, provided the Defence understands it very well, namely, that the Defence counsel should, in their cross-examination, limit themselves to the Defence counsel only whose accused are being mentioned by the witness with a view of a speedy and efficient trial. With your permission, Mr. President, let me link very briefly this issue with an issue you mentioned last week, for we believe that these two are very closely linked issues. I'm referring to the need for the indictment to be structured very well and very precisely. If we understood you well, at that time, you were addressing the Prosecution, and you emphasised that this also applies to the Defence. And when mentioning the Tadic case, you said that the Defence should be very precise as far as the questions of persecution are concerned. It seems to me that you said on that occasion that even in the event of a murder as an element of persecution, that it should also be very clearly defined as such in the indictment. Your Honours, we are now facing an indictment that has not been structured accordingly, which was very well observed by you, Mr. President. And as long as the indictment is structured in this way, the Defence and the Defence counsel, specifically, since we have the indictment, including Count 1, where the plural is used where the accused are indicted together with a number of other persons, we have to resist this sort of indictment as it is. We, therefore, take it that this indictment refers to everyone and to all of them. We believe that this stems from Rules of Procedures and Evidence, Article 82A, which indicates that in joint trials, each accused shall be accorded the same rights as if such accused were being tried separately. This is why we would urge you, Your Honours, to request the Prosecution to restructure the indictment. Here, we are speaking about very serious charges with very serious punishment implied, and we believe that those rules, which are relevant to very serious charges and punishment, these should be considered restrictively, and they should only apply to the facts that are very clearly specified. Where the indictments are not individualised, we believe our rights should remain such as they are, namely, that the Defence, indeed, insists upon the rights of the accused. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder whether the Prosecutor would like to comment on these remarks?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution does not share the views that have just been voiced by the Defence counsel. Would you like us to express ourselves this very afternoon on these, rather, general matters, or should we have a special hearing on these matters? I just wish it to be noted that we do not share these views, that we are at Your Honours' disposal to express our position, and if you wish us to do so now, we will be glad to do so. But we would like to hear your further guidance on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We feel it would not be advisable to deal with this problem this afternoon, perhaps next Monday or Tuesday before beginning with a new witness. Therefore, I think it is better to postpone the debate on this matter, but in the meantime, the Prosecutor could, perhaps, consider its positions on the matter. First of all, I would like to thank Mr. Pavkovic for his comments. Let me make, in a tentative way, very tentatively, because what I'm going to say will, in no way, prejudge the final position of the Court after hearing both the Prosecution and the Defence, just two points as follows: The first point, actually, when I asked the Prosecution and the Defence to try to file a supplementary brief, supplementary in the case of the Prosecution, on the notion of persecution, I merely expressed doubts. I didn't set out a definite position of the Court on the notion of persecution. I said that this is a difficult area, a new area where we have to break new ground, and it will be very important for the Defence and the Court to be aware of the position taken on this important legal issue by the Prosecution. By the same token, we would also welcome any legal brief from the Defence. The second point is, just expressing now my own view, I would say that I think at this stage it is impossible to ask or it is very difficult to ask the Prosecution to restructure the indictment, as you suggested. They may probably cast light on some points which are now being discussed and better define their position, in particular, the notion of persecution. I would agree with you. I don't have the indictment here close at hand, but I think that Count 1 relates to all indictees. To the best of my recollection, as you rightly pointed out, it does relate to all indictees. To this extent, of course, you're right to say that you have a right to cross-examine witnesses with particular respect to that count. In light of Rule 82A, again, I agree with you that this is the relevant provision, but let me sum up the discussion by saying that we are aware that we have to strike a balance between two notions or two requirements, the requirement of fairness and the requirement of expeditiousness of proceedings. Now, fairness means that we have to safeguard, by all means, the rights of the accused, particularly in light of Rule 82A. On the other hand, we should be mindful of this other basic requirement of expeditiousness, and that means that we want to avoid any unduly protracted proceedings. If the proceedings are too protracted, I think this is against the basic right of the accused to have a quick trial. Therefore, we wonder whether Defence counsel, when they feel that they have to ask questions in the cross-examination of witnesses, they could confine themselves to relevant questions, to questions which are relevant and not repetitive. My feeling has been so far that on many occasions, many questions put by legal counsel while cross-examining the witness were repetitive, were actually variations on the same theme, as it were, sometimes, say, on the discrepancy between the written statement and the statement made here in court by the witness. We don't need to hear about this theme ten times. I mean, we are a court of professional Judges. We do understand the points made so ably by legal counsel, and we, of course, as I say, don't need to -- we can't accept a sort of harping about the same theme in a repetitive manner. We would also like to ask, and these are two minor practical points, when you, Mr. Pavkovic, give us the list of legal counsel wishing to cross-examine the witness, could we say that the list should be, in a way, a final list? I do understand that you may have, at the last minute, one of the counsel who wants to put a question, but if possible, we would like to have a list which is complete without any last-minute additions. Also, I wonder whether you could stick to a principle that you yourself set out and proposed, and I think it's quite sensible, namely, that the witness should be first cross-examined by the legal counsel whose client is concerned by the testimony given by the witness. I think it's a more rational and logical principle, but on some occasions, I have realised that you have not followed this principle, as I say, enunciated by yourself. Having said so, we decided in a discussion at lunch time, that in future, we will try to be absolutely sensitive to the rights of the Defence and, on the other hand, also, however, be rather strict, and we may stop and ask you whether a particular question is relevant, so that you have to show why the question is relevant. This is sort of a practical arrangement, but let us see whether we can proceed in a more expeditious manner in the future. We also feel that, on some occasions, probably the Prosecutor should direct the witness, in a sense, to shorten the exposition of the witness. We do understand there are psychological reasons why some witnesses tend to talk at length because there is also, of course, a -- we all understand for what reasons. Probably one of the raison d’être of our Tribunal is also to enable witnesses to recount their own dramatic experiences. However, sometimes probably the Prosecutor may feel it opportune and advisable to try to lead, in this sense, the witness. Let us continue and hope that this afternoon we may move on to our next witness. I wonder whether there are other questions by Defence counsel. If not, I assume Mr. Radovic was the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, we have no further questions. Mr. President, we will certainly abide by your comments and suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's most helpful and kind of you. I would like to ask the Prosecutor whether he would like to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Moskowitz:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, just a couple of matters I would like to clarify with you. You were asked about the machine gun in front of the Papic house when you returned following the October '92 incident. You talked about a machine gun that could have a platform, in which case it would be an anti-aircraft gun, or this is a machine gun that could be used without a platform, in which case it would not be an anti-aircraft gun. Do you recall whether the machine gun you saw in front of the Papic house on the day you described had a platform or did not have a platform?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. The microphone is not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecutor is actually misleading the witness by putting these questions, because in his statement, the witness stated that the machine gun consists of the part which is used for shooting and the platform. And when it is used as an anti-aircraft gun, then another support is being used.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we know this specific machine gun. This is why it is not correct to say that the machine gun is used with a platform only when used as an anti-aircraft carrier or machine gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry. Can you stop? I think the question was whether the machine gun he saw on that particular day did have a platform or did not. I think it's quite appropriate, that particular day. Yes, Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: No, because the Prosecutor said, "This is a machine gun only when used with a platform." A special support has to be used as an anti-aircraft weapon. Without this special support, it is a simple machine gun that can be served and operated by only one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Can you rephrase it, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What I suggest is that the witness describes the gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Ahmic, describe the weapon that you saw that day?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: The weapon that I saw that day was a machine gun which can be fired by a single person. A single person can use this light machine gun. It can be operated by only one person. There was no platform. I saw no platform. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say it can be operated by one person. Can one person carry it easily?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. One person can carry it easily and can fire with it very easily. Because I was the person in charge of firing when using these machine guns in my military service with the JNA. But, of course, if it is used with a platform, you need three persons. The machine gun would be operated by the person who operates it and by somebody who helps him in firing, but it can also be operated by one person only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also were asked about whether or not you saw a flash of firing coming from the Ivo/Dragan Papic house. I want to clarify that, if we can. As you were fleeing from your house and before you were injured or shot in the elbow and in your side, did you see flashes coming from the Dragan Papic house or did you not?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: When I was crossing the road, I turned left and I turned right. When turning right, I noticed two soldiers bending close to Dragan Papic's house. At that time, I saw a flash from Dragan Papic's house, and then I continued running away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that flash appear to be coming from inside the house through one of the windows or from outside the house where the soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: It appeared to be coming from the window. I saw, actually, a shape behind the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were inside Hilmija's house, having been injured, were you able to see any flashes or any kind of firing coming from the Papic house?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. I was wounded. I was lying down, and I didn't see anything. I, actually, couldn't see anything. I was lying down until UNPROFOR took me out on a stretcher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, that ends my redirect, but I have a request at this moment to make of the Court and to ask the Court's indulgence on a third topic which would not, in my view, be proper redirect in that it was not raised on cross-examination. It is, however, I think, a point of clarification that may be helpful to the Court. There was some testimony briefly, I think, on direct about a sister-in-law who claimed to have seen a motorcycle with a BiH flag driving by. I think that was in response to a question about, "Did you see anything unusual on the 15th that made you suspicious that something was afoot," and I think that was one of the things that he mentioned. This is not a big point in the case. However, I have been informed by the witness that that is, in fact, not what he intended to convey. Rather than make a proffer in front of him as to what he intended to convey, he was quite adamant with me that having come all the way from Bosnia, he wants the record to be straight on what he intended to say. This is not, I think, narrowly redirect. So I raise it with the Court and seek the Court's advice about it. It don't think it's a major point. Although, you never know. As the evidence comes in, it may make some difference. In any event, he feels strongly that he wants to make it clear to the Court what he meant by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask Mr. Radovic. No comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that this is re-examination, so I'm wondering why this addition to the cross-examination, because if the Prosecutor intends to continue with the re-examination, let him continue without telling the witness what he intends to question him about in continuation of his re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. We have decided that Mr. Moskowitz may ask this question of the witness in re-examination. However, I think it is only proper for the Defence, if they feel the need to put questions on this very point, to ask questions of the witness in cross-examination. Please, ask the question of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you clarify, if you will at this time, what your, I believe it was, sister-in-law told you she saw? I'm now talking about that motorcycle on the 15th with, you say, the BiH flag on it.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. When my sister-in-law came to my house, she explained to me that she had seen two HV soldiers on motorcycles carrying around a Bosnian flag, the flag of the BiH army that was attached to the motorcycles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she tell you whether this flag was on the motorcycle or was it being dragged behind the motorcycle, or was it affixed in some other way?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: They were dragging it behind the motorcycle, along the road. It was being dragged along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I think that's the clarification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pavkovic, does any Defence counsel wish to cross-examine on this particular point?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radovic? Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here we are again the two of us, but I have just one question for you. These two who were pulling the Bosnian flag along the ground, have they got any connection with any one of the accused? Did you see any one of the accused doing such a thing?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radovic. I have only one question. This morning, Mr. Ahmic, this morning you said when -- and I have the transcript in front of me -- that when you were wounded and then treated by the UNPROFOR soldiers who came to see you, and they dressed your wounds and gave you an intravenous infusion, you asked them to be transferred to the hospital. And then you said there was an interpreter with them, and this interpreter said that they were not allowed to help anyone because those were the orders they had received from the Croatian army, and then they left. So my question is: Who told you that the Croatian army had issued orders to the effect that nobody should be treated in this hospital, if this is what you meant? You said, "helped." Who said so to you? Was the interpreter -- the interpreter said to you that the orders were that the -- from the Croatian army was that nobody should be helped in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the interpreter who told me that they mustn't assist our people, our wounded, that they mustn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Assist in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no. This was when he was giving me first-aid, when he was dressing the wound. This UNPROFOR officer and the interpreter in this house when they treated me for the first time, that is what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. But to which particular hospital were they referring? When you said, "Take me to a hospital," and they said "No, because we know of orders from the Croatian army." Were you thinking of a particular hospital?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't thinking of anything in particular, I was just trying to get saved. I was wounded and all I wanted was to be taken away, because there was no help coming from any side. There was no one who could help us except for the UNPROFOR. And what they did was to halt the shooting and take the women and children towards the upper village. We had no other aid coming from any other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, if the Registrar could be so kind, or the usher, as to give the witness Prosecution Exhibit number 80. I wonder -- this is a picture showing you in the house of Mr. Hilmija Ahmic. I wonder whether -- yes, it should be put on the ELMO. Could you please indicate who of these two UNPROFOR soldiers, I don't know whether they are both soldiers, one is interpreter, who told you that you could not be taken to the hospital because of the orders received from the Croatian army?

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: I know that the interpreter said this to me, and I think that this is the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: We have another photograph which we didn't introduce, only because we didn't want to be duplicative, that, I think, shows the two men more clearly if it would be of assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No. Thank you. It's sufficient, because clearly one -- their uniform is slightly different. Anyway, so this young man, the interpreter, who you called the interpreter, told you about the Croatian orders. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ahmic. I assume there's no objection to the witness being released? Mr. Ahmic, thank you for coming here to testify in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FAHRUDIN AHMIC
utterances.text: Thank you, you too. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Now, the while the Prosecutor is calling the next witness, may I raise, very quickly, an issue to which we would like to draw the attention of both parties? The important remark and request made yesterday in court by Judge May about the need to see, to be aware and have a clear perception of the distances between the various buildings, houses, the mosques, the cemetery, the Catholic cemetery and so on, set us thinking of the problem of whether it would be feasible for the Court to do what we call a visit to the site of the alleged crime, which is provided for in many International Tribunals, including the International Court of Justice, and we came to the conclusion that this would be extremely useful to the Court to have an idea of the village, the small village. This is provided for in our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 4, which states as follows: "A Chamber may exercise its functions at a place other than the seat of the Tribunal, if so authorised by the President, in the interests of justice." I have also looked up the relevant rules of the Statue and Rules of Procedure of the International Court of Justice. They also provide for the same possibility and give some guidance. We strongly feel that it would be important for the Court to go there. However, we feel that it will be good to go with the Defence counsel and the Prosecutors, and without the accused, because this may create problems for the accused to go there, quite a few problems. But probably the presence of Defence counsel, all Defence counsel, will be sufficient. And we could try to see whether we could spend this one day, one full day, moving around, checking the various buildings and so on. Of course, we know there are two problems. One problem is security for those people, say, Defence counsel, the Prosecutor and the Court to go in there, plus members of the Registry, security and financial implications, which is always a huge problem. Before, however, formally sending a request to the President and the Registrar, we would like to have your views and know whether you, in principle, would be in favour. If so, we could send, as I say, a request to the President and the Registrar, more so because I think the area is under control of the Dutch/American forces, members of UNPROFOR, and probably the Dutch army or whatever forces could provide for transportation from here, and maybe a military aeroplane with all the Court, including, of course, the parties and so on. And probably one full day there would be sufficient. This would, of course, in a way, make also the financial implications acceptable, and they or the other forces of UNPROFOR should provide security to all of us. What is the position of the Prosecutor first, and then the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would most sincerely applaud the idea that you just proposed. We believe that it is, indeed, very important for this trial in particular to know exactly the site. I went on several occasions and saw that for myself, how important it was, after reading the documents. So I do indeed think it is very important, that it is an excellent idea in principle. As for the practical aspect of the matter that you referred to, I think there is no doubt that your Court will receive the full co-operation and support of the Dutch battalion SFOR, which is responsible for the Vitez region. There will certainly be a number of practical problems to deal with, security problems, for example, the mine -- problem with the mines, to make sure that the mines have been removed, but I think that not one of those problems is insoluble and they can all be overcome. As for the legal formalities, the legal aspect of this move, as far as I am concerned, and according to my experience, it is something that is done very frequently and doesn't pose any problems, and one has to ensure the contradictory aspect of the trial, that is that the Defence should be present, and I see no major obstacles. Therefore, the position of the Prosecution is very favourable regarding your proposal, despite the absence of the accused. As far as I know, there is nothing about that in the rules, but I think the contradictory nature of the trial will be ensured by the presence of Defence counsel of each of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: As far as we are concerned, we also agree with this proposal and we feel it would be useful. As far as your security is concerned, from the Croatian side, we can assure you that there is absolutely no danger, as far as we are familiar at least, with the mentality of the people living in Vitez and in the environs. Therefore, we accept and we do believe that this will contribute to an objective assessment of the events in that area for what is happening in this trial. In this trial, we had already, in the investigation stage, asked the investigators to come to Vitez, and not to interview only one side and not to only indict on one side. You have an indictment that is absolutely one-sided. Not a single person from the Croatian side was heard. So this will be the first step towards establishing a balance. And the next step, of course, will be, when you hear the second group of witnesses, that is the Defence witnesses. I must say, unfortunately, that for the first time in my career as an attorney, before I was a Judge, it was the first time that I come across the problem of, "My witnesses and your witnesses," because in the area in which we worked, we usually had witnesses of the Court, a person who has to tell the truth regardless of whether he is speaking in favour of the Defence or the Prosecution. He conveys what he saw and what he heard. We realise that this system was established when the International Court of Justice -- no, I'm sorry, not the Court of Justice, for the crimes in the former Yugoslavia was established. But in any event, we applaud this step which will ensure that things are viewed not in a one-sided manner only. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the point of, "Our witnesses, their witnesses," I'm afraid this is the procedure. And this is, of course, as you know, Mr. Radovic, better than me, it is the adversarial system, which is totally different from the inquisitorial system with which you are familiar in your country and also other European persons from Continental Europe are also familiar with namely the inquisitorial system where you have a totally different approach, but we have to stick to our rules. Therefore, we have the Prosecution witnesses and then in a few weeks time we will have the Defence witnesses. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course, this is up to you to decide when we'll be going on this trip to visit the site, but it seems to me that I can speak of behalf of my colleagues in the Defence, that after the presentation of the Prosecution evidence, that would perhaps would be the most convenient moment to visit Ahmici. That is, between the Prosecution and the Defence case. At the end of the Prosecution case and before the beginning of the Defence case. That would be my suggestion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for asking for the floor again, but when deciding on the date of this visit, one must bear in mind that this is Central Bosnia, and that the weather in the later autumn is quite harsh, and already in December it can snow because the altitude is quite high. I'm just drawing your attention to this technical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: But I think Mr. Pavkovic made a very good point. The best period would be after the Prosecution case, the end of the Prosecution case, and before the Defence start with their own case, namely in October. And October is the period of the first episode, the first attack, so, therefore, it would be quite appropriate. So we would also be aware of -- become aware of the weather in October. All right. Well, I thank you for your comments, and, of course, on the basis of your position, which is in favour of our suggestion, we will send a formal letter, a request to the President and the Registrar. We will now move on to the next Prosecution witness. (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Akhavan. Could you make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I shall speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Now, this is typical witness where probably the Prosecution could focus on a few major points. Also, because we have the statement. May I ask, Mr. Terrier, do you regard Mr. Akhavan as an expert witness or as a fact witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution considers Mr. Akhavan as a fact witness, which means he will be cross-examined by representatives of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan could you tell the Court your name and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I name is Payam Akhavan. I was born on April 11, 1966.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you're working with the Office of the Prosecutor for the International Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell the Court about your education and experience in the area of International Humanitarian Law?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I have obtained a law degree and a post-graduate law degree in the field of International Human Rights Law. Prior to joining the Tribunal, I had worked with the Norwegian and Danish Human Rights Institutes respectively in Oslo and Copenhagen, after which I joined the United Nations Centre for Human Rights, where I worked with Tadeusz Mazowiecki. Prior to that I'd been involved in the missions of the Conference of Security and Cooperation in Europe, both of which were related to humanitarian law violations in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, you participated in the preparation and drafting of a report of the Human Rights Commission, dated 19th May, 1993, under the heading, "The Situation Regarding Human Rights on the Territory of the Former Yugoslavia"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to tender into evidence a copy of this report. I wish to say, Mr. President, that this is a public document that, of course, the witness is not a signatory of it. It is a report of the Commission for Human Rights, of which Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki was the head as the former Prime Minister of Poland. We have communicated through a representative of the Defence and tendered a copy of this report, though it is not, strictly speaking, a statement of the witness, but we have given a copy of this report to each of the Defence counsel. If they wish, I can give them additional copies if they need them. In any event, I am at the disposal of the attorneys.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 82.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, could you explain under which circumstances you participated in the drafting of this report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I was a member of the staff of the Special Rapporteur for the former Yugoslavia, Prime Minister Mazowiecki, and was deployed in Zagreb together with a college, (redacted). We were approached during the middle of April by the members of the European Community Monitoring Mission regarding allegations that humanitarian law violations had taken place in the Lasva Valley region of Central Bosnia and, in particular, in the village of Ahmici. Both of us had also seen television footage of atrocities which had been committed in this village. At that point, we decided to obtain approval from the United Nations Centre for Human Rights in Geneva in order to conduct an on-site investigation. After which we arranged, through the United Nations Protection Force, to travel to the Lasva Valley region, upon which we conducted extensive interviews with members of the British battalion, with members of other international agencies such as the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the ECMM, as well as those who had survived the events in Ahmici. This report reflects the findings of that mission, in addition to information coming from other sources, relating, for example, to the city of Mostar and other events which we did not directly investigate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding the facts on Ahmici, which you did investigate, could you tell us, roughly, what was the date, if you remember, or how many times you went to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We arrived in the town of Vitez on the 30th of April and left on the 7th of May. So we were there approximately one week. During this period, we visited Ahmici on three occasions, I believe, on May 1st, 2nd and 6th. During this period, we also once visited the survivors of the attack on Ahmici in the neighbouring city of Zenica, in addition to conducting interviews with some of the commanders who may have been involved in that attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us comment on your visit to Ahmici, please. Could you tell us what struck you, in particular, in this village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The scale of destruction was quite extensive. I believe that from approximately 150 to 200 homes in the village, there were fewer than 20 which had not been destroyed. The scale of destruction was extensive. There were homes which, some two weeks after the attack, were still smouldering. There was also a real, what would I describe as, smell of death in the village. One could sense that there were still many bodies which had not been recovered from underneath the rubble. There was virtually not a living creature in the village. Even dogs, cats, and cattle had been killed and were lying all over the roads. So I think on the whole, what struck me was the total and all-embracing form of the destruction of this village and its inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you, with the permission of the President, approach this aerial photograph showing the village of Ahmici, and with the pointer on your left, indicate the area of the village which you specifically visited during the several visits that you made to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I will simply describe the various locations which we visited on the three occasions, not necessarily indicating the order in which they were seen. This, I believe, is the road from which we arrived. We visited the area immediately adjacent to the Catholic cemetery, because according to some of the members of the British battalion who had escorted us to this region, this field right here was an area in which several bodies, up to 20 bodies, had been recovered. Their impression was that this so-called "killing field" was where a number of people who were escaping in a southerly direction from the north of the village may have been ambushed. We checked this small hollow, which is adjacent to the field, and noticed that there were a large number of spent shell casings, indicating that this area may have been used as a staging area for the ambush by the snipers. We travelled up this road to the area where the mosque had been destroyed. This is the mosque with the minaret, because there were two mosques, one further up the road, I believe, in this area. Here we inspected the damage to the mosque and the destroyed minaret and did a small survey of the neighbouring homes in order to appraise the extent of the damage. We also went further up the road, as I explained, to the upper mosque, which had been gutted by fire, and on another occasion inspected some of the homes in this area, as well as a bit further up the road. That, I think, is more or less the areas of the village which we visited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding what the members of the British battalion called the "killing fields," it is the field that you pointed to adjacent to the Catholic cemetery; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Adjacent to the Catholic cemetery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what the members of the British battalion told you regarding the bodies that they found in that field? Were they combatants, civilians, men, women or children?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: According to the members of the British battalion, the 20 people who were found in this so-called "killing field" were almost exclusively women and children, with possibly also some elderly individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Close to this "killing field," to use the term coined, you found traces of ammunition, ammunition shells, shell cases. Can you tell me what kind of weapons were in question?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: When we did the survey of the various homes, we counted, on average, anywhere from 30 to 50 spent shell casings around the homes, indicating that a considerable amount of ammunition had been used in the attack, also indicating that much of the ammunition was used in the immediate proximity of the home rather than at some distance. The ammunition included the spent shell casings of bullets which would ordinarily be used in machine guns, but we found also some spent shell casings which, according to the British battalion, belonged to anti-aircraft guns. These weapons were used, on occasion, in attacks on personnel, although they were not intended for that purpose. We also found remnants of what I would call grenades which are shot from -- I forget the name of the weapon. Well, they're grenade launchers, and they have rather big shell casings. We also found some of those. I believe that there were also, in certain cases, empty or broken bottles which were apparently used to carry petrol or gasoline or other flammable liquid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you examine the insides of some of the houses to have as detailed an idea as possible of how these homes were incinerated?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We inspected a number of homes. The impression which we gathered is -- well, clearly that the homes were set on fire. There were various reasons why we came to that conclusion.
