For one thing, the nature of the combat was not such that homes would catch on fire, let's say, because of cross-fire or the use of heavy weaponry. The attack was predominantly by means of guns, which would normally not result in homes going on fire. But what impressed us the most was the intensity of some of the fires and the manner in which certain parts of the home were burnt, to the point where there was a black shine on the wood, suggesting that the fire was one set by the use of gasoline or some other flammable liquid. As I said, virtually every home, with the exception of maybe 15 or 20, had been destroyed by means of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your various visits to Ahmici, you accompanied representatives of the British battalion of UNPROFOR. Did you encounter inhabitants of Ahmici in Ahmici during the course of that visit to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. We encountered an elderly woman with two young children, who could have been her grandchildren, possibly, walking through the village. We approached her in order to see if she would be willing to speak to us about the events which transpired in Ahmici on April the 16th and if she could possibly help us identify some of the perpetrators. At this point, we noticed that there was sniper fire coming in our direction, indicating that someone was not happy with us speaking with this lady. So we had to leave that area and go immediately back to the armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would now like for us to talk about the encounters you had with some of the survivors who were chased out of Ahmici and whom you met with in Zenica. Could you tell this Tribunal where these survivors were located from Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The survivors were located through the assistance of an institution in Zenica which, I believe, was the centre for the collection of evidence on genocide and war crimes. I believe that this was a governmental agency, although I'm not sure. They identified the location where 150 survivors of Ahmici, who had been detained in a school in Dubravica, I believe, by the HVO, were located. I believe the location was possibly a cinema or some other large community centre which was being used temporarily as a refugee centre. We met there with about 50 or 60 of the survivors of the Ahmici attack. Almost all of them were women or young children, with a few elderly males in their midst. We asked them about the events which had transpired on that date, having spent several hours speaking with them, trying to see whether the stories coming from the different individuals were consistent or not. Almost all of them gave roughly the same description of the attack, suggesting that it had commenced very early in the morning around the time when the morning call to prayer had taken place at the minaret, that the attack had begun through explosions towards the north of the village which, presumably, was the result of a mortar attack, and that subsequent to that, there had been heavy gunfire, soldiers going from door to door indiscriminately shooting at buildings. Very often there were stories, accounts, of people being taken out of homes and executed. There were accounts of petrol being poured in the floor of homes or being thrown through windows and homes set on fire. One small girl recounted how her father had been lured out of their home on the promise that he would not be harmed and how he had been shot as soon as he left his home. There were accounts of various instances of killing. I think that I remember only one or two cases where people managed to escape because a member of the HVO decided not to kill them. There was one lady whose husband had been killed, and apparently the perpetrator knew her from before and had decided to spare her life, and he had simply told her that she should rush off and save her life, and that he would not harm her. We wanted to make sure that we would know the identity of the perpetrators. Of course, we were not involved with a criminal investigation. We were human rights investigators. We were involved in the attribution of liability to a state or, where a state does not exist in the context of such an armed conflict, the de facto authorities which exercised authority over that region. Almost all the survivors, without exception, told us that the soldiers were wearing HVO uniforms with the distinctive insignia of those armed forces. We tried to make sure that the soldiers were not members of another paramilitary formation, such as HOS or the others who were operating through the region. What convinced us that this attack was, indeed, committed by the HVO was the fact that, even in the short amount of time that we had, the witnesses came up with the names of 18 perpetrators, all of whom they knew by name, because they were either their own neighbours or people whom they knew from neighbouring villages. At that point, we were convinced that the HVO, indeed, had been responsible for the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a man whose name was Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Sakib Ahmic, correct. The gentleman in question was interviewed by my colleague, (redacted) (redacted), on the following day, I believe, in a hospital in Zenica where he was recovering from burns which he had sustained on his body. According to the testimony of Sakib Ahmic, he had been hiding in the back of a couch when the HVO units had attacked the home of either his son or daughter, I don't recall, but he was staying at the home of one of his children. He had heard gunshots, after which he saw the man and woman of the house fall to the ground. There were also two children in this home, according to him, one an infant of less than six months, and another a child of three to four years. He said that after hearing the gunshots, and while he was not certain if the people had actually been killed by the gunfire or not, that the HVO soldiers began to pour petrol over the home, after which he set the home on fire, not knowing that he was hiding behind the couch. He managed somehow to escape through a window and to arrive at Zenica where he was treated for very bad burns which he had sustained on his hands and feet and the side of his body. Based on his testimony, we revisited Ahmici, I believe, on the 6th of May, together with three European Community ambassadors from Spain, France, and Britain respectively, who were on a diplomatic mission to try and stabilise the situation in the Lasva Valley region. We went to the home which Sakib Ahmic had described, based on a crude map which he had drawn on a piece of paper, and we found the home, and indeed, we also found the bodies of the four individuals. There were clearly two adults. One of the bodies was simply a vertebra and a skull. Another body still had the rib cage attached, but the bodies, in general, were not complete. But one could tell that there were two adults. Then there were the remains of what appeared to be an infant and a child, although they were so badly burned, that only with great care was it possible to understand that they were actually human beings. At first, we thought maybe they were some fabric or something else which had been burnt. I believe that after our visit, members of the British battalion took these bodies and gave them a proper burial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I request that we be able to show a video, which is a news real made by Scan News made on 6 May, 1993 during the time of the visit which Mr. Akhavan and (redacted) made to Ahmici. This was, of course, with the British battalion, a film which this Tribunal has not had the opportunity yet to see, but this is something that we would like to show Mr. Akhavan now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This brief film was not shown at that particular time, but I hope, nonetheless, that this video will be tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, and the Trial Chamber, of course, have the opportunity to see that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 83.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, during that mission in Central Bosnia, in order to clarify what exactly happened, did you meet with the political authorities or military authorities from the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes, we did. During the day that my colleague went to meet Sakib Ahmic in Zenica, I went to meet with the leading authorities of the HVO in the Lasva Valley region. I met first with then Colonel Blaskic at his headquarters in Vitez, after which I met with Mario Cerkez, who, I believe, was the head of the HVO in Vitez. After that, I met with Dario Kordic, who was the vice-president of the HVO and the HDZ political party, I believe, in the Herceg-Bosna community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among these various political and military authorities, did you ask of them what might have happened in their own assessment in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. The purpose of the meetings was to try and see whether there were any plausible alternate theories or explanations as to what may have transpired in Ahmici. None of the people with whom we spoke admitted that the HVO were involved in these crimes. To the contrary, they insisted that the HVO, being professional soldiers of high rectitude and conduct, could not be involved in such terrible actions, but there were no plausible alternative explanations offered. Dario Kordic, at one point, tried to suggest that the Serbs may have committed this crime or that Muslim extremists themselves may have committed the crime in order to gain international sympathy. None of those theories were plausible, in light of the consistent and overwhelming testimony of the witnesses with whom we had spoken, and in light of the fact that Ahmici was, perhaps, only two kilometres away from the HVO military headquarters in Vitez. It would have been exceptionally difficult, for example, for a group of Serbs to cross the lines undetected, numbering in the vicinity of 50 to 100 soldiers, and to commit such an attack undetected. So after those meetings, we were further confirmed in our conclusion that this was an attack perpetrated by the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you advise those Croatian authorities with whom you met of any conclusions from your own report?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: We had not yet prepared the report. Naturally, we were still in the course of gathering the necessary facts. After the report was issued, I believe that it was circulated to all the appropriate sources, including, for example, the government of the Republic of Croatia, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We did not formally give this report to the authorities in the Lasva Valley region, since it was not really our mandate to do so. We submit these reports to Geneva. After an editing process, they become official documents of the Commission for Human Rights. At that point, there is a standard distribution of these documents to the member states of the Commission for Human Rights, and so on and so forth. But I do know that the authorities in Herceg-Bosna did ultimately receive this report, and I know this because they sent a letter, a long letter, to Tadeusz Mazowiecki criticising the report, suggesting that it was one-sided, suggesting that it was inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did these Bosnian Croat authorities conduct an investigation regarding what happened in Ahmici in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I was aware that there was discussion of an agreement between the Bosnian government side and the Bosnian Croat side suggesting that they were willing to undertake an investigation. To the best of my knowledge, no such investigation ever took place. Certainly, we did not hear of any individual being prosecuted or punished for the events in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the Croat contacts make mention of any loss of life among the Croats or damage to any property owned by Croats in the Lasva Valley on that date of the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: With respect to the village of Ahmici, no. None of the authorities which we met suggested that there was any sort of property damage or casualties among the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Outside the village of Ahmici, did you learn of any other losses suffered by Croat inhabitants, outside the village of Ahmici in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: There were two occasions where we came across Croatian casualties. In the city of Vitez, we were told by the padre of the British battalion that a few days ago they had buried 101 individuals who had been killed in the fighting in Vitez. Of those 101 people, 96 were Muslims and five were Croats. In the case of a small hamlet called Miletici, which was a few kilometres away from Vitez, we came across evidence that certain renegade elements, popularly referred to as the Mujahedin, had come to this village and apparently beheaded three or four young Croatian men of fighting age in that village. So the evidence which we had is that, for example, in the case of Vitez, that some Croats may have been killed in the cross-fire or in the actual fighting that was occurring in Vitez because, indeed, the Muslims did control one part of the city. In the case of Miletici, we saw what appeared to be a random act of violence by criminal elements, but the case of Ahmici, I think, could be distinguished. There was very little evidence, if any, that there was any sustained or organised military resistance in Ahmici, as distinguished, for example, in Vitez, where even two weeks after the events of April the 16th, the Bosnian Muslims still controlled part of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened in Ahmici, as you described, did this occur after the 16th of April, 1993? Did that happen later in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did what happen after April 16th? The visit to Miletici or the events in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The events which took place in Miletici, did they take place after the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. Our impression was that the killings were in retaliation. I believe that it was after April the 16th that the killings in Miletici took place, but the killings in Vitez took place during the fighting, I believe, on and after April the 16th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to be very clear and to be clear about your personal intervention and also the meaning and significance of your report, your objective, I'm speaking now about the human rights report, was it designed then to find out who was responsible, individual responsibility, or to just make a report about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: The report, as I had explained earlier, was not to attribute individual criminal liability, but was to establish the responsibility of the entity which should bear liability under international law for those human rights violations. The mandate of the human rights special rapporteur in such a situation is to determine the responsibility of state authorities for particular violations. In the case of an internal armed conflict or an international armed conflict where there is a disintegration of state authorities, and it's not possible to attribute liability to a state in the ordinary sense, then one looks at those authorities which exercise a de facto control over a given area, irrespective of their status as a state or other entity. In this case, the entity which we were involved with was the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna which exercised the de facto powers of a government or state in that territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To place this into a certain context, on the date of that report, when it came out, this Tribunal did not yet exist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions. I would simply wish to submit or tender a number of documents to the witness and also to this Court. These were taken on the 6th of May or during the days that followed, perhaps the 7th of May. These photographs were taken by the members of the BRITBAT from UNPROFOR, and these are photographs taken in the house of Sakib Ahmic. These are photographs taken of the cadavers found in those houses. Some of these photographs will, perhaps, call for a commentary from the witness, but perhaps a brief commentary.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 84.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at these photographs that are going to be shown to you rather quickly and comment on those which you think deserve commenting? Do you recognise the things that you were able to see with your own eyes when you visited that house of Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. This is the body of one of the adults which we found in the home which Sakib Ahmic had described in an area which was probably the living room or a bedroom. I'm not sure. All the walls had collapsed in the home. It was difficult to tell. This was the body which, as I explained, still had the rib cage intact, whereas the other body still only had the vertebra and the skull. It seemed as if the body had not yet fully decomposed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the photographs that are being shown to you require no commentary, please just confirm that they were all taken in Sakib Ahmic's house.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 85.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: This is probably the body of either the infant or the child, based on its size and the fact that it was burned very badly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 86.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this still another photograph taken in the home of Sakib Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that that is the room in which we found all of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are all the objects that we see on the floor there?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe that those were the shingles which were used on the roof of the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next photograph, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 87.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe that that is the same rib cage of the adult which we had seen earlier. I presume these were the members of the British battalion that came after our departure in order to take the bodies away and to give them a burial. Once again, the body of one of the adults. These, I suppose, as I explained, are the British battalion members putting the bodies in nylon bags so that they could be taken away and buried, still in the same home as I described earlier. I think we've already viewed this picture.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the bodies that were found in this house were taken by the British battalion, where they were transported and buried?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I'm not certain in this particular case, but, in general, bodies were taken to Zenica where autopsies were performed in the morgue. I'm not sure in this particular case where they were taken. This, once again, I believe, is one of the bodies of the children. This is probably the body of the infant, given the size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you speak of the smallest child, you mean an infant, the child of the age of an infant, a baby. Does that conform with what Mr. Sakib Ahmic had told you previously?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: That's correct. Once again, by the size, I believe that this should be probably the infant, given the size. Of course, it's very difficult to tell, because the bodies were burnt so badly, and in many cases, bits and pieces of the body were missing. So the size can sometimes be misleading.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the object on the photograph, at the same time as the human remains, allows us to judge the size of the remains. Next photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, we entered this room from this door here, and the bodies of the adults were towards this end of the room, and the body of the infant and the child towards this end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the threshold that we see at the top of the photograph, is that the entrance into the house?

utterances.speaker: PAYAM AKHAVAN
utterances.text: I believe it's the entrance into this room of the house. My impression was that the actual entrance was located somewhere here, but I'm not entirely sure of that. Once again, I'm assuming this is remnants of the child, probably not the infant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: We have no more photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, that was the last, and the number is 69.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could 82 to 96 be admitted into evidence? And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it is too late for the cross-examination, so we will now adjourn and resume work tomorrow at 9.30.
